content: Ribose, commonly observed in its D-ribose form, is classified as an aldopentose. This means it is a monosaccharide that contains five carbon atoms and features an aldehyde functional group in its linear structure. Its chemical formula is C₅H₁₀O₅. Ribose was first identified in 1905 by Phoebus Levene. Ribose plays a vital role in biological systems as a fundamental component of RNA, which is essential for genetic transcription. It is closely related to deoxyribose, the sugar found in DNA. Additionally, ribose is a key structural element in several critical biomolecules, including ATP (adenosine triphosphate), NADH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), and other compounds integral to cellular metabolism. For further details on the relationship between ribose and deoxyribose, as well as their roles in genetic material, refer to discussions on deoxyribose. In terms of isomerism, D-ribose shares the same stereochemical configuration at its penultimate carbon atom as D-glyceraldehyde, a simpler monosaccharide.
